title: CERT-In names 'Crafty Falcon' as AI hacking tools linked to China hit Indian lenders
dek: India's cyber agency says the group uses freely available AI tools to break into non-bank lenders, fintechs and crypto exchanges at machine speed. Researchers have tied at least two of the tools to China.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
India's cybersecurity agency has given a name to the attackers behind a run of break-ins at non-bank lenders, fintech firms and cryptocurrency exchanges: "Crafty Falcon", a group it says uses freely available artificial intelligence (AI) hacking tools to carry out whole attacks "at machine speed". At least two of those tools have been linked by security researchers to China.

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) rated the threat "critical" in an advisory first issued on Wednesday and updated on Friday. "The threat is active and ongoing," it said, adding that some firms that had already fixed the holes flagged in earlier warnings had been attacked again, often over holidays and weekends when fewer staff were watching.

## What the advisory says

The advisory, numbered CIAD-2026-0058, says the name was given by CSIRT-Fin, CERT-In's unit for the financial sector. It describes Crafty Falcon as an "AI-assisted financial threat actor" and lists the entities it has gone after: non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), digital lending platforms, fintech firms, payment aggregators, payment service providers, and cryptocurrency exchanges and other virtual digital asset providers.

It names four tools seen in the attacks: the "ARTEX" family of tools built on large language models, PentAGI (described as an autonomous multi-agent penetration-testing system), Cairn (an attack search engine) and the CyberStrikeAI framework. CERT-In calls them "publicly available AI-driven offensive security tools", and notes that they "do not validate authorization", meaning they will attack any system they are pointed at.

The advisory itself does not name any country or say who runs Crafty Falcon. The first report on the advisory said CERT-In did not identify the operators or where they are based, and did not describe the attacks as state-sponsored. The China link comes from outside researchers' work on the tools, not from CERT-In.

According to the advisory, the attackers:

- got in through test and staging systems left open to the internet, then used shared passwords or access tokens to move into live systems
- took apart and modified firms' mobile and web apps to send money-moving instructions directly to their servers
- abused cloud management services to run commands and plant files
- sent Rs 1 "test" transfers to check that a route worked before moving large sums
- misused payment aggregators' merchant settlement systems to move money out
- stole the private keys of cryptocurrency wallets
- exploited newly published software flaws within a short time, and generated large numbers of custom scripts, which CERT-In links to AI-assisted development

## Where the China link comes from

ARTEX is the tool most closely tied to China. On 7 October the US security firm CrowdStrike said a campaign against South Korean banks from late September had used ARTEX, which it described as an open-source penetration-testing tool developed in China, together with commercial AI models. CrowdStrike assessed with "moderate confidence" that the attacker was a single Chinese-speaking, financially motivated operator, and said its evidence was not enough to identify the person conclusively, according to reports. One report said at least nine South Korean banks had disclosed or been reported as targets.

The same report also said that CrowdStrike had linked a China-linked group to the use of ARTEX in an espionage campaign against more than 200 organisations in at least 14 countries, and that ARTEX's developer made the tool private last month after it was tied to the Korean attacks.

## Beijing's position

China has not commented on the Indian advisory, which does not mention it. When asked about the CrowdStrike findings on 8 October, foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said: "China consistently opposes and cracks down on hacking activities in accordance with the law," adding: "We are even more firmly opposed to the spread of misinformation for political purposes," one report said. She said the ministry did not know the specifics of the case.

## Background

Friday's advisory builds on an earlier one. On 9 October CERT-In warned, in advisory CIAD-2026-0046, that attackers were stealing the credentials that let lenders send instructions to their partner banks, then calling disbursal and transfer systems directly from the victims' own trusted servers. That skipped checks such as KYC, sanctions screening and limits, and sent money to mule accounts at several banks for quick withdrawal. It said some signs pointed to "AI-assisted offensive tooling". That advisory was also updated on Friday.

Two Mumbai-based non-bank lenders lost about $2 million in more than 700 unauthorised instant transfers from ICICI Bank accounts on 8 and 9 October, according to a police complaint described in one report. The complaint said hackers had compromised the link used to send loan-disbursal instructions. CERT-In has not said which incidents it attributes to Crafty Falcon or how much has been stolen.

Other bodies have raised the alarm too. On Tuesday the Home Ministry's Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) warned banks and fintechs that AI agents were being used to steal "crores of rupees". The Reserve Bank of India has asked banks to show evidence that they meet cybersecurity requirements and to assess security gaps in the software links they share with non-bank lenders and fintechs, one report said last week, citing sources.

## What firms are told to do

CERT-In's list of measures is long. The main ones are:

- 24-hour monitoring, with lower alert thresholds during holidays and weekends
- keeping test systems fully separate from live systems, with no shared passwords
- treating customer apps as untrusted, and checking every transaction on the server
- fixing internet-facing software fast, with a web application firewall as a stopgap
- flagging a Rs 1 test transfer to a new beneficiary followed by a large transfer, and adding cooling-off periods
- requiring two people to approve merchant settlements
- keeping crypto wallet keys in hardware security modules or cold storage, with multi-signature withdrawals
- banning unauthorised offensive AI tools on company systems

Incidents are to be reported to CERT-In and to the Cyber Fraud Mitigation Centre.

## Why it matters

India's digital lending and payments business runs on exactly the kind of system-to-system links that Crafty Falcon is abusing: lenders, fintech apps and payment aggregators sending instructions to partner banks. The attacks show that tools able to run a break-in largely on their own are now freely available, and that smaller lenders and fintechs can be reached through weaker links even when big banks are well defended. For customers, the risk is mainly to the firms' money and data; CERT-In has not reported losses from individual accounts.

The episode also adds to India's concerns about its digital dependence on China. Even where no state is involved, tools developed in China and released openly are now being used against Indian financial firms, and India has little say over how such tools are built or distributed.

## What happens next

CERT-In says the campaign is continuing, and it is likely to update the advisory as more indicators emerge. The RBI is pressing banks on the security of their links with partners. Firms hit by an attack must report it within six hours under CERT-In's 2022 directions.
